title: 16-year-old American Payton Westcott to represent Mercedes in 2026 F1 Academy season
content:
Payton Westcott’s dream has always been making it to Formula 1. And now, she is taking a crucial step forward as she prepares to race in F1 Academy.

Mercedes announced on Monday that the 16-year-old American driver will represent the Silver Arrows in the all-women racing category, a junior racing series that uses a car similar to Formula 4.

Westcott, who made her F1 Academy debut at the 2025 Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend as a wild card driver, will compete for PREMA Racing and will continue racing in Italian F4 this year.

Westcott was born and raised in California and began driving go-karts aged six, at the Thermal Club. Her father would drive cars at the well-known motorsports club, and Payton said to The Athletic, “He put me in a go-kart when I was very little, because it was kind of like the babysitting. He didn’t really expect it to turn into anything.”

One of her earliest motorsport memories is her first time in a go-kart. While she was taught how to use the brake, throttle and steering, she did not  know what the flags meant.

“So I went out and I was doing laps, and then they started waving the checkered flag because they wanted me to come in, and I didn’t come in,” Westcott said. “I just kept going around and around. And then eventually it happened so much that they had to go out on track and get me to come back into the pits.”

It was another three years before driving became more serious for Westcott. She received her first go-kart at nine years old, hence why she races under the number nine. But it wasn’t until she was 12 years old that her family discovered “go-kart racing actually existed because out at that track, it was only just driving. There wasn’t any racing.”

Westcott’s competitive racing story started with national karting series, like the United States Pro Kart Series and the California Pro Kart Challenge. She achieved third in the Challenge of the Americas and spent three years competing in karting categories, taking a step into international competition in the final year. In 2024, she received an F1 Academy ‘Discover Your Drive’ scholarship and competed in the Champions of the Future Academy Program, which featured three European races and three Middle Eastern races.

It was Westcott’s mother “who found out about the Discover Your Drive program,” Payton said, and it proved to be instrumental in her career journey. Through the program, Westcott met her manager (though not directly) and learned more about the European racing scene.

“I did three races in Europe, and that’s when we realized we had to go to cars as soon as possible,” Westcott said. “So I moved about a month later, to Italy, and I moved October 3, 2024, and started testing in cars.”

Considering her California roots, one may wonder why Westcott is pursuing the F1 ladder rather than IndyCar. She explained that it was down to her family’s passion for racing and how they routinely watched F1 during her childhood.

“I remember my dad asked me where I wanted to go, and that was my only answer,” Westcott said. “So that’s also played a major role into why we decided to move to Europe, because if we were to stay in the U.S., we would most likely be going the IndyCar route.”

Her family still resides in California, but Westcott says her parents travel with her “as much as possible,” with her mother and father essentially trading out. She said that living part-time in Europe has been a major adjustment and also had to deal with a jump in the level of competition between U.S. karting and European karting. With the switch, she also needed to change engine and chassis categories, as well as age categories.

“The gap, from cars and karts, while it might look similar in the idea, it’s completely different,” she said.

Last season, Westcott competed in multiple single-seater categories, including the Formula Winter Series, Italian F4 Championship and the E4 Championship and also took another two big steps in her F1 Academy journey. She was one of the drivers to participate in the category’s inaugural rookie test and set the fastest time in the afternoon session, ultimately finishing in the top three of the overall results.

She went on to make her F1 Academy debut in November, competing as Visit Las Vegas’ wild card entry in the season finale, allowing Westcott to demonstrate her abilities in equal machinery.

Gwen Lagrue, Mercedes’ driver development advisor, said that Westcott’s results in Italian F4, Euro 4 and the UAE Formula 4 series “underline not only her speed but also her ability to adapt quickly to highly competitive environments.”

“The 2026 season will be intense for Payton,” he said in the news release. “We believe this dual program will accelerate her progression and provide a solid foundation for her long-term ambitions in single-seater racing.”

Westcott faces big shoes to fill given that her predecessor, Doriane Pin, won last year’s F1 Academy title. Pin is remaining with Mercedes as one of its development drivers this year, while also competing in her own racing program, and part of her role will be supporting Westcott this season.
